title: China's CXMT says new memory-chip platform enters mass production
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Chinese memory manufacturer ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) says its fifth-generation DRAM platform has entered mass production, a milestone that could narrow China’s gap with leaders Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron.

DRAM stores the working data for processors in smartphones, computers and servers. Unlike NAND flash, it is volatile: information disappears when power is removed. Performance, energy consumption and cost depend heavily on how densely manufacturers pattern each memory cell and how efficiently wafers yield usable dies.

CXMT says its platform reduces feature spacing to 11.95 nanometres through quadruple patterning. This technique splits a circuit layout across several lithography and deposition steps, creating finer structures than a single exposure can resolve. It is technically demanding because every stage introduces alignment, defect and process-control challenges. However, successful implementation can raise transistor density without requiring the most advanced extreme-ultraviolet lithography equipment.

The company also introduced 24-gigabit LPDDR5X chips for smartphones and portable electronics. Each device stores 50% more data than earlier 16-gigabit products, while LPDDR5X is designed to deliver high bandwidth at low voltage. CXMT claims the platform produces at least 50% more gross dies per wafer than its previous generation, potentially lowering unit costs if manufacturing yields remain strong.

Why does this matter? First, mass production signals repeatability, not merely a laboratory demonstration. Second, higher density and wafer productivity could make CXMT a more credible supplier to Chinese electronics brands, reducing reliance on imported memory. Third, domestic process development helps China work around restrictions on advanced foreign semiconductor tools.

The broader impact could extend beyond China. Additional DRAM capacity may intensify price competition in a notoriously cyclical market, pressuring incumbent manufacturers’ margins. Yet CXMT’s claims still require independent validation. Commercial success will depend on yield, reliability, power efficiency, customer qualification and the ability to scale output consistently across millions of chips globally.
